## Incident Report — PCAP: 2026-01-31-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap

**Evidence file:** `2026-01-31-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (SHA256 `f755444d0b6eac847e07b73dea0774084b232d8577f536547a12f39b959d7833`), 51,181 packets, 2026-01-28 03:04:03–03:14:27 UTC. No IDS/Suricata alert exports were present in the evidence directory — only the pcap.

### Victim host
| Field | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 | 10.1.21.58 | source of all suspicious traffic; only non-infrastructure local host on the /24 (peers were only 10.1.21.1 gateway and 10.1.21.2 domain controller) |
| MAC | 00:21:5d:c8:0e:f2 | ARP: `10.1.21.58 → 10.1.21.2` and Ethernet source on all frames from 10.1.21.58; also seen self-announcing on link-local 169.254.227.202 |
| Windows hostname | DESKTOP-ES9F3ML | DHCP option 12 hostname, and NBNS registrations `DESKTOP-ES9F3ML<00>/<20>` from 10.1.21.58/169.254.227.202 |
| AD domain | win11office.com (NetBIOS WIN11OFFICE, DC WIN-LU4L24X3UB7) | DNS SRV lookups for `_ldap._tcp...win11office.com`, NBNS `WIN11OFFICE<1e>` |
| Logged-in user | gwyatt | Kerberos `CNameString` on AS/TGS exchanges between 10.1.21.58 and DC 10.1.21.2 |

### Malware family
**Attribution: behavioral, not signature-confirmed** (no IDS alert data was provided in the evidence directory to confirm a name).

The traffic shows a classic fake-download/traffic-distribution-system (TDS) infection chain rather than a single well-known commodity malware signature:

1. `hiyter.com` (t=45.3s) → `media.megafilehub4.lat` (t=45.8s) → `arch.filemegahab4.sbs` (t=48.3s, resolved to 104.21.46.67/Cloudflare) — a "mega file hub"-style fake software/file-download lure. This flow to 104.21.46.67 is the single largest conversation in the capture (~16 MB downloaded), consistent with a malware payload/installer being pulled down; the session is TLS 1.3 with Encrypted Client Hello, so the payload itself, its filename, and hash cannot be recovered from this capture.
2. `whooptm.cyou` (t=90.3s) — brief TLS session with rapid small application-data exchanges, consistent with a secondary loader/gate check.
3. `whitepepper.su` (t=92–122s) — a fingerprinting/tracking gate. In plaintext HTTP (port 80) the victim's browser was served injected JavaScript that harvested a full browser fingerprint (WebGL renderer, canvas fingerprint, screen/resolution, installed fonts, audio stack, plugins, hardware concurrency, `navigator.platform=Win32`) and POSTed it back to `/api/set_agent?...&act=log`, tagged with a persistent `id` and `token`. This gate/fingerprint-then-log pattern is characteristic of malvertising/ClickFix-style TDS panels that route victims to fake-update or fake-CAPTCHA pages before dropping a stealer or RAT.
4. `holiday-forever.cc` (t=122.8s) and `communicationfirewall-security.cc` (t=126.5s) — final redirect hops; the latter's naming (fake "communication firewall/security" theme) is consistent with a fake Windows security-warning lure page typically used to social-engineer execution of the payload.

Given the .lat/.sbs/.cyou/.cc bulletproof-style domains, the fingerprint-gate-then-redirect structure, and the large encrypted payload pull, this matches the behavior of a fake-download/malvertising TDS delivery chain (the pattern most associated with campaigns like LandUpdate808/KongTuke-style gates) used to drop a stealer or loader. No file could be recovered to name the final payload family with certainty, so it is reported as **behavioral attribution: fake-download/TDS-gate malware delivery chain**, not a confirmed named family.

### Indicators of Compromise

**C2 / gate endpoint:**
- `153.92.1.49:80` — `whitepepper.su`, fingerprinting/check-in gate (plaintext HTTP `GET/POST /api/set_agent`)

**Malicious/suspicious domains (all resolved and contacted by 10.1.21.58):**
| Domain | Resolved IP | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| hiyter.com | 104.21.22.231, 172.67.207.145 | DNS query at t=45.3s, first hop in chain |
| media.megafilehub4.lat | 104.21.48.156, 172.67.154.67 | DNS query t=45.8s |
| arch.filemegahab4.sbs | 104.21.46.67, 172.67.136.13 | DNS query t=48.3s; correlates with 16 MB TLS/ECH download from 104.21.46.67 |
| whooptm.cyou | 62.72.32.156 | DNS query t=90.3s, TLS SNI=whooptm.cyou |
| whitepepper.su | 153.92.1.49 | DNS query t=92.3s; plaintext HTTP fingerprint-collection gate |
| holiday-forever.cc | 80.97.160.24 | DNS query t=122.8s |
| communicationfirewall-security.cc | 104.21.9.36, 172.67.141.109 | DNS query t=126.5s |

**Malicious URLs (observed in plaintext HTTP):**
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome`
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome&act=log` (POST, exfiltrates full browser fingerprint JSON)
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Edge` (repeated with second UA)
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Edge&act=log`

**File names / hashes:** None recoverable. The only large transfer (≈16 MB from `arch.filemegahab4.sbs`/104.21.46.67, the probable payload/installer) occurred entirely inside a TLS 1.3 session using Encrypted Client Hello; no decryption keys were provided, so no filename or SHA256 could be extracted from the capture. All plaintext HTTP objects recovered (`connecttest.txt`, `favicon.ico`, the `set_agent` fingerprint pages/JS) are non-executable and benign in themselves.

### Benign context (not IOCs)
Standard Windows/Microsoft/Google/Bing/MSN telemetry, OS update, and CDN traffic: `*.events.data.microsoft.com`, `client.wns.windows.com`, `login.live.com`, `login.microsoftonline.com`, `*.googleapis.com`, `www.google.com`, `www.bing.com`, `www.msn.com`, `cdnjs.cloudflare.com`, `static.cloudflareinsights.com`, `assets.adobedtm.com`, `www.msftconnecttest.com` (NCSI), plus internal AD/DC traffic (LDAP, Kerberos, DRSUAPI/LSARPC, SMB2, NBNS) between 10.1.21.58 and the domain controller 10.1.21.2.

### Incident summary
Windows workstation DESKTOP-ES9F3ML (10.1.21.58, MAC 00:21:5d:c8:0e:f2), domain win11office.com, logged in as user **gwyatt**, browsed a chain of fake file-hosting/download lure sites (hiyter.com → media.megafilehub4.lat → arch.filemegahab4.sbs) and pulled down a ~16 MB encrypted payload, then was routed through a browser-fingerprinting check-in gate at whitepepper.su (POSTing full device/browser fingerprints under a persistent id/token) before hitting further redirect domains (whooptm.cyou, holiday-forever.cc, communicationfirewall-security.cc). This is consistent with a fake-software/malvertising TDS delivery chain used to drop a stealer or loader; the exact payload family cannot be named with certainty since the download itself was TLS-encrypted with no keys available, so attribution is behavioral only.
